messages.subject: Applicability of R-INLA in complex SPDE-governed cases
parts:
Hello,

I stumbled upon the R-INLA package (and the nice papers) and wondered whether it is/you see it applicable in the following scenario:
I would like to apply it e.g. to fluid dynamics cases where the flow is governed by the Navier Stokes equations, i.e. (S)PDEs which do not have a analytical solution. Meaning, that I assume to have sensory readings e.g. from a river at certain positions and would like to estimate/predict the parameters at other positions of the river. As possible simplification, I could also possibly assume the flow to be stationary such that I'm only interested in spatial field.

In this regard, my questions are:
  1. Do you generally see R-INLA fit in this case?
  2. How can/should I deal with the SPDE I face (I guess that I can use some simplifications to the general Navier Stokes equations but those still don't have an analytical solution) ?
  3. Assuming I have found a solution to question 2 (e.g. in the extreme case saying that I don't care about the actual SPDEs governing my system and instead use the models available to R-INLA), how can/should I deal with boundary conditions?

Thanks a lot for your help in advance.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Applicability of R-INLA in complex SPDE-governed cases
parts: On 15 January 2018 at 08:15, 'Herbert Meier' via R-inla discussion

group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> I stumbled upon the R-INLA package (and the nice papers) and wondered
> whether it is/you see it applicable in the following scenario:
> I would like to apply it e.g. to fluid dynamics cases where the flow is
> governed by the Navier Stokes equations, i.e. (S)PDEs which do not have a
> analytical solution. Meaning, that I assume to have sensory readings e.g.
> from a river at certain positions and would like to estimate/predict the
> parameters at other positions of the river. As possible simplification, I
> could also possibly assume the flow to be stationary such that I'm only
> interested in spatial field.

The answers depend on where you want to have the stochasticity; in the
parameter fields, in the PDE driving terms, or both.
The SPDEs in R-INLA are all linear SPDEs driven by random noise, and
the dimensionality of the parameter fields is practically limited.
The case of random field parameters for deterministic PDEs doesn't
really match what we've done at this point, and it falls more under
the "UQ" umbrella (though some of the methods are still applicable).

> In this regard, my questions are:
>
> Do you generally see R-INLA fit in this case?

See above; linear SPDEs with small degrees of freedom (largest I've
tried was dim = 16) are fine. Nonlinear SPDEs are not.

> How can/should I deal with the SPDE I face (I guess that I can use some
> simplifications to the general Navier Stokes equations but those still don't
> have an analytical solution) ?

If you can construct a linear finite element approximation, then the
INLA method can be applied.

> Assuming I have found a solution to question 2 (e.g. in the extreme case
> saying that I don't care about the actual SPDEs governing my system and
> instead use the models available to R-INLA), how can/should I deal with
> boundary conditions?

Any boundary condition that you can build into the finite element
construction is fine; we nearly always use Neumann boundaries due to
their simplicity, but by extending the domain away from the domain of
interest, boundary effects are moved away so that they affect the
analysis less (or not at all). The best/easiest approach is problem
dependent.
the "rgeneric" method can be used to define ad hoc models of this
type, but for specific PDE operators (e.g. involving flow vector
fields), extending the existing fmesher software for the FEM analysis
is a better long-term option.
In any case, it's a research project.

Finn

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com>
Date: 15 January 2018 at 11:31
Subject: Re: [r-inla] Applicability of R-INLA in complex SPDE-governed cases
To: Herbert Meier <hello.ti...@googlemail.com>


On 15 January 2018 at 11:00, 'Herbert Meier' via R-inla discussion

group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>> The case of random field parameters for deterministic PDEs doesn't
>> really match what we've done at this point, and it falls more under
>> the "UQ" umbrella (though some of the methods are still applicable).
>
> Thanks for pointing this out!
> I would consider the stochasticity in the PDE driving terms.
> Out of curiosity, could you tell me what "UQ" stands for such that I could
> browse some details for this?

UQ = "uncertainty quantification". It's the term used by the applied
maths and "inverse problems" community. It's essentially statistics by
another name...

>> See above; linear SPDEs with small degrees of freedom (largest I've
>> tried was dim = 16) are fine. Nonlinear SPDEs are not.
>>
> Thanks! I guess I would then need to investigate techniques to linearize the
> governing equations.
Yes. Though with N-S I imagine that's not easy!

> In computational fluid dynamics, finite difference methods are often used
> instead of finite element, would this also work with R-INLA?

Yes, finite differences are fine if you can use them.
The key is that you need to be able to construct the precision matrix
(inverse covariance) of either values at nodes (for finite
differences) or basis function weights (for finite elements).

> As I'm not (yet) familiar with R-INLA, could you elaborate or point me to
> some sources how this linear FEM approximation could be used in R-INLA and
> in which format it needs to be provided?

A user defined "rgeneric" model needs to provide a precision matrix;
search r-inla.org for rgeneric examples, which I believe are there.
You may want to read up on the general GMRF theory and practice (the
GMRF book by Rue and Held 2005 is a good start).
Also the Lindgren, Rue, Lindström 2011 JRSSB paper says more about the
FEM/SPDE/GMRF connection.

> For my understanding: Is it correct that e.g. the Navier Stokes (S)PDEs play
> only a role in the co-variance function of the random field generating
> points?

If N-S had been linear, yes. The nonlinearity leads to non-Gaussianity
(even if it were driven by Gaussian noise), which means that the model
isn't fully defined by expectation and covariance alone.
A linearised and Gaussian model _is_ however fully defined by its
expectation and covariance (or precision).
Whether that's the only influence of the specific (S)PDE that is used
is up to your specific model.

> Again for my understanding: The boundary conditions again affect only the
> co-variance functions of the random field generating points, right?

I'm not sure what you mean by "the random field generating points".
But the boundary conditions only affect the covariance function of the
random field, yes, if that's what you meant.

Finn
